strengths: The paper offers a clean, well-motivated conceptual framework: it defines a formal notion of 'world model' via consistency/sensitivity properties over prompt-intent pairs, then relaxes this into a practical 'sufficient world model' definition using an evaluator function, which is a sensible way to make an abstract philosophical question operational.

The variance decomposition (PS/AS/MU, summing to one) is intuitive, interpretable, and provides a principled way to disentangle sources of response variability -- a real methodological contribution beyond simple accuracy or scalar prompt-sensitivity metrics used in prior work (e.g., PSS, FormatSpread).

The empirical study is reasonably thorough: 5 domains, 15 base tasks, 5 models spanning different sizes/families, with bootstrap confidence intervals reported for every decomposition estimate, and a robustness check using an alternative (survey-style) prompt generation method in the appendix.

The paper situates itself carefully relative to closely related work (stochastic parrots critique, prompt robustness/spurious-features literature, and especially Vafa et al.'s DFA-based world-model test), clarifying what is genuinely new about the distribution-aware, evaluator-tunable approach.
The appendix extension to discrete/categorical outputs via an information-theoretic (entropy/mutual-information) analogue is a nice generalization that broadens applicability beyond numeric tasks.

Honest reporting of mixed/modest findings (larger models not uniformly better, domain-dependent robustness) rather than overselling the result, and discussion of practical implications (fairness auditing via Articulation Sensitivity) is a plus.
weaknesses: Nearly the entire evaluation pipeline (translation-based paraphrasing, intent-preservation verification, and numeric answer extraction) is delegated to GPT-4o-mini with no human validation or inter-rater checks; errors or biases introduced at any of these stages could confound the PS/AS/MU estimates, and this is not empirically assessed.

The operationalization of 'intent change' in most tasks is simply varying a single numeric slot in an otherwise fixed template (e.g., income level, number of boxes, mg of medication). This is a narrow and somewhat mechanical notion of 'purpose,' arguably closer to testing numeric input-sensitivity/interpolation than to testing a rich notion of user intent as motivated in the conceptual sections.

Reducing free-form model responses to a single extracted scalar discards most of the information in the response and privileges tasks with a well-defined 'bottom-line number,' which narrows the class of tasks to which the method can be applied and may bias which failures/successes are visible.

The central empirical claims (larger models generally have higher PS) are weak and inconsistent across domains and models (e.g., 70B is not uniformly best, Gemma 27B sometimes underperforms Gemma 12B), and the paper does not provide a formal cross-model/cross-domain statistical test of these comparisons, relying instead on visual inspection of bar charts.

In most reported tables, Model Uncertainty (MU) dominates the decomposition (often >0.7-0.9), meaning PS and AS -- the terms motivating the entire framework -- are frequently small, limiting the discriminative power and practical significance of the diagnostic in the tested settings.

Only a handful of models (five) and a single model per size tier are tested, and the alternative survey-based paraphrase generation is only validated for two models/four domains in the appendix, leaving open whether the qualitative conclusions are robust to the specific choice of models or paraphrase-generation method.

The heavy formal notation in Section 2/3 (world model definitions, sufficient world model, R^2-based decomposition) is essentially reformulating a one-way ANOVA/variance-components model; while pedagogically useful, the level of formalism may overstate the technical novelty relative to the (conceptually simple) underlying statistical method.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually clean and interpretable framework: decomposing LLM response variance into Purpose Sensitivity, Articulation Sensitivity, and Model Uncertainty, with a clear identity (PS+AS+MU=1) that is easy to interpret and communicate.

The formalization progresses logically from an idealized 'world model' definition to a more tractable 'sufficient world model' definition with an explicit evaluator, and the paper is thoughtful about the philosophical distinctions (e.g., consistency vs. correctness, Remark 2 on outdated-but-consistent models).

The related-work section carefully positions the contribution relative to prior work on world models in RL/games (Vafa et al., Toshniwal et al.) and prompt-sensitivity literature (ProSA, FormatSpread), clarifying what is genuinely new (variance-based, distribution-aware, non-oracle-dependent evaluation).

The experimental design includes a reasonably rich set of controls: cross-lingual back-translation for generating articulation variants, semantic-equivalence filtering, diverse prompt selection via embedding distance, bootstrap confidence intervals for all reported statistics, and a secondary survey-based prompt-generation method as a robustness check.

An extension to discrete/categorical outputs via an information-theoretic (entropy/mutual-information) analogue is provided in the appendix, showing the framework's potential generality beyond numeric tasks.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is weak and largely undercut by the paper's own results: the abstract asserts larger models have 'more robust world models,' but the text repeatedly concedes the 70B model is not consistently better, its advantage is 'often modest,' and it even shows *higher* articulation sensitivity in some domains—leaving the paper without a clear, well-supported takeaway about what drives world-model quality.

The measurement pipeline depends heavily and non-trivially on GPT-4o-mini at multiple stages (translation, intent-equivalence filtering, and numeric answer extraction), yet there is no human validation or error analysis of these LLM-as-judge/extractor components, so measurement noise or systematic bias from GPT-4o-mini could be conflated with the target models' 'world model' properties.

The task suite is narrow (15 base tasks across 5 domains, all requiring numeric point-estimate answers) and appears partly hand-constructed to elicit large purpose-driven swings (per Remark 3), raising construct-validity concerns about whether results generalize to typical open-ended LLM usage beyond quantity-estimation prompts.

The definition of 'intent' (Remark 1) is model-relative and somewhat circular—two prompts share intent if they 'elicit the same output distribution from the model'—which makes the operationalized metric partly definitional rather than an independent, falsifiable test of understanding, and the 'sufficient world model' notion is highly sensitive to the arbitrary choice of evaluator τ̂ and V with no sensitivity analysis on this choice.

Only two model families (LLaMA, Gemma) and five model sizes are evaluated, limiting the generality of any size-related claims; no larger frontier models (e.g., GPT-4/Claude-class) are tested, and cross-family comparisons (e.g., why Gemma 27B sometimes underperforms Gemma 12B) are not analyzed in depth.

Model Uncertainty (MU) dominates the variance decomposition in the vast majority of reported cells (often >0.7–0.95), meaning the headline PS/AS differences that the paper emphasizes are typically small absolute shares of total variance; the paper does not adequately discuss how this dominance affects the reliability or practical significance of the PS/MVS comparisons across models.

Statistical rigor across models is limited: the paper reports bootstrap CIs per model/task but does not perform formal significance testing for between-model differences in PS, AS, or MVS, despite drawing directional conclusions ('larger models attribute a greater share...') from what are sometimes overlapping intervals.

strengths: Clean, interpretable theoretical framework: the PS + AS + MU = 1 variance decomposition is mathematically well-motivated (via standard R^2 decomposition) and yields an intuitive 'signal-to-noise' (MVS) summary statistic that is easy to communicate to practitioners.

The paper carefully develops two nested definitions (a strict 'world model' and a more usable 'sufficient world model' relative to an evaluator), and situates this work thoughtfully against related literatures (stochastic parrots critique, RL world models, DFA/Myhill-Nerode based evaluation of Vafa et al., prompt-sensitivity/format-robustness literature), showing good scholarly awareness of adjacent work.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: 5 domains x 3 tasks x 5 models x 3 intent values x 50 paraphrases x 50 samples, with bootstrap confidence intervals reported per task/model in the appendix, and a secondary survey-style paraphrase generation method used as a robustness check that yields qualitatively similar patterns.

Honest and nuanced reporting of findings: rather than overselling a clean 'bigger is better' story, the paper reports that improvements from scale are inconsistent across domains and often modest, and explicitly flags this as a limitation rather than smoothing it over.

Extension to discrete/categorical outputs via an information-theoretic (entropy/mutual-information) analogue of the decomposition broadens applicability beyond purely numeric responses and shows the framework's generality.
Practical framing connecting AS to fairness/dialect robustness concerns is a plausible and valuable applied motivation for the metric.
weaknesses: Substantial gap between the rich, abstract notion of 'intent' motivated in Section 2 (e.g., the coin-flip/positive-negative equivalence example) and its actual operationalization in experiments, which reduces to varying a single numeric slot in an otherwise fixed template (income level, box count, medication quantity). This is closer to testing sensitivity to an explicit input variable than to testing whether the model infers a latent, unstated communicative goal, which is a weaker and less novel claim than the framing suggests.

The Model Uncertainty (MU) term dominates in nearly all reported results (often 0.6-0.95 of total variance, per Tables 1-5), meaning the headline PS/AS comparison is being made over a small residual share of the total variance; the paper does not discuss how this affects the reliability or interpretability of cross-model PS/AS comparisons, nor does it test whether observed PS/AS differences across models are statistically distinguishable once MU's dominance is accounted for.

Only 15 base tasks total (3 per domain) with only 3 discrete intent values each; this is a small and somewhat ad hoc task set from which broad claims about 'world models' across five real-world domains are drawn, limiting generalizability and statistical power, especially given the observed inconsistency across tasks/domains/models.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o-mini for three separate roles (paraphrase generation via translation, intent-equivalence verification, and numeric answer extraction) introduces compounding, uncharacterized noise and potential systematic bias into the pipeline; no human validation of paraphrase fidelity or extraction accuracy is reported, which is a reproducibility/soundness concern given these judgments are central to defining what counts as 'same intent' and to computing the response values used in the decomposition.

The evaluator V collapses rich free-form responses to a single scalar per response (with ranges averaged and non-numeric responses discarded), discarding substantial information the model may encode in its answer; this is acknowledged as a limitation but its practical impact on the reported decomposition (e.g., bias introduced by discarding indefinite answers) is not empirically probed.

No proprietary/frontier models (e.g., GPT-4/4o, Claude, Gemini) are evaluated, only open-weight Llama and Gemma variants up to 70B, limiting how much the scaling conclusions generalize to state-of-the-art systems most relevant to 'high-stakes' deployment claims made in the introduction.

The central empirical finding is fairly modest (larger models are only somewhat, inconsistently better), which is honestly reported but also means the paper's demonstrated 'diagnostic value' is not strongly validated against any external ground truth of model quality or downstream task performance—there is no correlation analysis linking PS/AS/MVS to independently-verified measures of model competence or reliability.

strengths: Novel and well-grounded conceptual framework that connects LLM 'intent comprehension' to a formal variance decomposition (Intent Sensitivity, Articulation Sensitivity, Model Uncertainty), with clear ties to prior work on world models, Bayesian inverse planning, and Gricean pragmatics.

Careful, rigorous formalization: two nested definitions (strict and 'sufficient' intent comprehension), a principled R^2-based decomposition that sums to one, and a natural extension to an entropy-based analogue for discrete/categorical outputs (Appendix A.2), showing the framework generalizes beyond numeric responses.

Large-scale, carefully constructed experimental pipeline: 5 models (LLaMA and Gemma families), 5 domains, 24 tasks/domain, 10 paraphrases and 12 intents per task, 25 responses per prompt-intent pair, yielding ~1.77M model responses.

Methodologically thoughtful treatment of finite-sample bias in variance estimation via hierarchical/mixed-effects (ANOVA) modeling with partial pooling and bootstrap confidence intervals, rather than naive plug-in estimators.

Solid human validation of the two key pipeline components (paraphrase intent-preservation and numeric extraction accuracy), with reasonably high raw agreement rates and transparent reporting of confusion matrices and chance-corrected statistics.

Useful derived summary metrics (MVS, ICI) with an interpretable precision/recall-like structure, plus robustness checks across temperature settings and an additional discrete-output case study (loan approval/risk rating) that reinforce the main qualitative findings.
Practically motivated discussion connecting the metric to fairness/dialect robustness and deployment risk assessment, which situates the contribution within meaningful real-world use cases.
weaknesses: The core paraphrase-generation method (multi-hop back-translation) may introduce systematic 'translationese' artifacts that are conflated with genuine articulation variation, so Articulation Sensitivity may partly reflect translation-pipeline idiosyncrasies rather than pure surface-form variation; no ablation isolates this confound (e.g., comparing translation-based paraphrases to human- or LLM-paraphrased-without-translation prompts).

Model coverage is narrow (only LLaMA and Gemma families, all open-weight, at most 70B parameters); the central claim that 'larger models attribute more variance to intent' is not tested against other major model families (e.g., GPT, Claude, Qwen, Mistral) or at larger scales, limiting generalizability of the scaling conclusions.

The operational definition of intent (Remark 2.3: two prompts share intent iff they induce the same response distribution) risks circularity — it defines intent equivalence partly through model outputs rather than an independent ground truth, so a model could score well by simply being globally low-variance/repetitive without any deeper 'understanding.'

The framework is explicitly correctness-blind (Section on Sufficient IC, Remark 2.5): a model that is consistently and confidently wrong scores identically to one that is consistently correct. While philosophically defended, this substantially limits the practical usefulness of the metric alone for deployment decisions, and the correctness extension is relegated to an appendix rather than empirically demonstrated in the main experiments.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4.1 throughout the pipeline (intent generation, translation, paraphrase equivalence filtering, and numeric-value extraction) introduces a validation loop where one LLM's judgments underlie much of the evaluation of other LLMs' 'understanding,' with only modest-scale human spot-checks (200 items, 2 annotators) to validate this.

Empirical results are acknowledged by the authors themselves to be inconsistent and modest ('gains are uneven and often modest with increasing model size'; smaller Gemma-12B sometimes outperforms larger LLaMA-70B), which weakens the strength of the paper's central narrative about model scale and intent comprehension.

The task distribution (open-ended Fermi/guesstimation-style quantitative estimation across 5 broad domains) is a fairly narrow and somewhat artificial slice of real-world intent-critical interactions (e.g., no coding, multi-turn dialogue, or instruction-following tasks), raising questions about how well findings transfer to more typical LLM use cases.

No direct empirical comparison against existing prompt-sensitivity metrics discussed in related work (e.g., ProSA's PromptSensiScore, FormatSpread), so it is unclear how much new signal the proposed decomposition provides relative to simpler existing measures.
